title: What the Doctor Didn’t Order: Informative Missingness as a Clinical Signal in ICU Prediction Models
content: Objective: Clinical prediction models treat missing data as noise to be imputed. In intensive care, missingness is not random—whether a physician orders a serum lactate or places an arterial line reflects diagnostic reasoning, workflow protocols, and institutional practice. We quantified how much predictive information resides only in the pattern of which measurements were obtained, entirely independent of their values.Materials and Methods: Using 84 013 ICU admissions from MIMIC-IV, we extracted binary missingness matrices indicating which of 113 clinical features were observed during the first 24 hours. Gradient-boosted models were trained on three tasks—sepsis diagnosis, hospital mortality, and vasopressor requirement—using missingness patterns alone, observed values alone, and both combined. Temporal validation separated training (n = 50,740), validation (n = 18,828), and test (n = 14,286) sets chronologically. Primary metrics were AUROC and AUPRC with bootstrap confidence intervals. Robustness was assessed via permutation importance, SHAP analysis, L 1 -penalized logistic regression, and comparison with SOFA and OASIS clinical severity scores.Results: Missingness-only models achieved AUROC 0.742 (95% CI 0.730–0.755) for sepsis, 0.710 (0.697–0.723) for mortality, and 0.810 (0.802–0.817) for vasopressor requirementcapturing 84–93% of values-only model discrimination and outperforming SOFA and OASIS on two of three tasks. In combined models, all 50 highest-importance features were missingness indicators rather than observed values, confirmed by SHAP and logistic regression. The top indicators were clinically coherent: absence of lactate and respiratory rate recordings for sepsis; absence of lactate and BUN for mortality; absence of invasive hemodynamic monitoring for vasopressor requirement. Adding explicit missingness indicators to imputed values producedno improvement (AUROC ∆ −0.001 to +0.001, all p > 0.05), because median imputationalready encodes missingness implicitly.Conclusion: What is not measured in the ICU predicts outcomes with discrimination approaching standard models. ICU prediction models partially learn institution-specific ordering behavior rather than novel physiology, with direct implications for cross-site generalizability. We propose reporting missingness-only baselines and monitoring missingness distributions during deployment to detect model–environment mismatch.
